For instance, Republican Eisenhower, wanting a conservative SC, named Earl Warren (former Republican governor of California) CJ and William Brennan associate justice -- but after maturing in their seats, the duo became leaders and inspirers of the progressives who redefined the Bill of Rights with libertarian decisions junking racial segregation, creating the right of abortion for women, and inventing the 'Miranda rights' of criminal suspects; asked over national TV what mistakes he made as president, the WWII hero Eisenhower quipped: 'Yes, two mistakes, and they are still sitting in the Supreme Court'

Presidents in the PH have also tried to influence the SC by selecting justices for perceived loyalty, not for philosophical or ideological orientation -- but like Eisenhower they too are often frustrated because, once ensconced in their seats, their appointees become independent as mandated by the Constitution; in CJ's humble view, presidents should not despair when their appointees perform constitutional duties with 'competence, integrity, probity and independence' -- rather, they should be proud because the people will appreciate, and history will vindicate, them for their prudent choices

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban opens by noting that his column last Sunday ('SC tops SWS poll,' C101) elicited -- aside from the usual Twitter-type, knee-jerk reactions -- lengthy and perceptive comments on the need to know the legal philosophy of Supreme Court justices. In that piece, CJP opined that in addition to the qualifications required by the Constitution, magistrates -- especially SC justices -- should (1) be industrious so they can help solve the recurring case backlog, and (2) have a philosophy of law so their decisions would be predictable and jurisprudence stable. CJP does not have the space to discuss in detail the interesting feedback from several lawyers, political scientists, and even a retired DLSU professor, Dr. Adelaida Lacaba-Bago, who related Lawrence Kohlberg's theory of moral development with legal philosophy and CJP's conversations with US Justices Antonin Scalia and Anthony Kennedy. But CJP refers them to 'Scalia, A Court of One' by Bruce Allen Murphy (published 2014 by Simon and Schuster, NYC) -- a 644-page book that labels Scalia as 'the most recognizable and most controversial member of the Court.' Scalia is berated or praised (critics are never neutral on him) for his 'originalism theory for deciding cases, believing that the Constitution and its amendments should be interpreted according to the meaning of the words as people understood them at the time they were written.' A high school valedictorian, top student at Georgetown, law review editor and magna cum laude at Harvard, Scalia is known for his 'unwavering adherence to the traditional Roman Catholic faith' with St. Thomas More as his model, and for his 'love for argument.' The US Court's most senior associate justice in length of service, Scalia (78) is viewed to belong to 'the same voting clique' as CJ John Roberts and two other 'conservative' justices. They follow the 'judicial restraint' doctrine espoused by the oft-cited Harvard guru, the late Justice Felix Frankfurter. They face four dedicated 'liberals or progressives' in the nine-member US Court. The swing vote is held by Justice Kennedy, also 78 and also Catholic (the religious faith of justices is minutely monitored in the United States, with five Catholics on board now), who frequently leads the liberals. Following tradition, Kennedy -- as the second most senior member -- is given the power of naming the decision writer whenever he sides with the four liberals and defeats the four conservatives. No wonder the current US Court is many times referred to as the 'Kennedy Court' rather than the 'Roberts Court,' in honor of this Stanford, London School of Economics, and Harvard Law (cum laude) alumnus, whom Scalia has 'belittled in so many earlier cases.' Perhaps to his chagrin, Kennedy is now endearingly called the 'shadow chief.' Even more than in the Philippines, the appointment of US SC justices is a politically-sensitive matter -- indeed, the ideological future of the federal judiciary is indubitably raised and decided as a tantalizing issue during US elections. During the 2008 presidential election campaign, Democrat Barack Obama boldly proclaimed that he favored 'somebody who's got the heart, the empathy, to recognize what it's like to be a young teenage mom; the empathy to understand what it's like to be poor, or African-American, or gay, or disabled, or old.' His opponent, Republican John McCain, promised to appoint 'conservative self-restraint jurists who would oppose liberal judicial activists.' True to his promise, Obama -- celebrating his stunning victory -- elevated two women liberals: Yale alumna Sonia Sotomayor in 2009, the first Hispanic and third woman to be named to the US SC, and former Harvard Law School dean and SG Elena Kagan in 2010. In 2013, Sotomayor affirmed her liberal roots in her best-selling book 'My Beloved World.' Historically, Democrats (Obama, Bill Clinton) tended to appoint liberals, and Republicans (Reagan, George Bush) favored conservatives. But their appointees sometimes overrule them. For instance, Republican Dwight Eisenhower, wanting to have a conservative SC, named Earl Warren -- former Republican governor of California -- CJ, and William Brennan associate justice. However, after maturing in their seats, the duo became the leaders and inspirers of the progressives who redefined the US Bill of Rights with libertarian decisions junking racial segregation, creating the right of abortion for women, and inventing the 'Miranda rights' of criminal suspects. After his term, Eisenhower was asked over national television what mistakes, if any, he made as president. The WWII hero quipped: 'Yes, two mistakes, and they are still sitting in the Supreme Court.' Presidents in the Philippines have also tried to influence the SC by selecting justices for their perceived loyalty, not for their philosophical or ideological orientation. But, like Eisenhower, they too are often frustrated because, once ensconced in their seats, their appointees become independent as mandated by the Constitution. In CJ's humble view, presidents should not despair when their appointees perform their constitutional duties with 'competence, integrity, probity and independence' -- rather, they should be proud because the people will appreciate, and history will vindicate, them for their prudent choices.
